title: Germany must relearn the language of power-politics
gist: Peter Sies argues Germany's post-1945 aversion to power has become a strategic vulnerability the Kremlin actively exploits, and that genuine anti-fascism now requires a return to Machtpolitik. His most consequential and least consensus claim: Germany should pursue a nuclear deterrent, ideally by acquiring a small arsenal from France or the United States - financed by German money in exchange for French fiscal relief, or by a 'golden cheque' to a transactional Washington.

themes.theme: Germany's power-aversion as an exploitable vulnerability

insights.claim: A senior German official at the European Commission described Friedrich Merz's own government as 'fascist' on the basis of its migration policy and rearmament programme, illustrating how German elite discourse treats German strength itself as the principal threat.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Internal elite resistance is a real constraint on German rearmament execution, not just a rhetorical flourish - defence procurement timelines should be discounted accordingly.
insights.quote: ‘This government is fascist’, a high-level German official at the European Commission in Brussels told me last year.
insights.locator: Opening: ‘This government is fascist’

insights.claim: Russia's sabotage strategy against Germany is specifically designed to stoke angst about escalation, weaken centrist parties and scare Berlin off military aid to Ukraine - on the calculation that if the German pillar cracks, European support collapses with it.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: German domestic politics is the single highest-leverage target for Russian influence operations; German coalition stability is therefore a leading indicator for all European Ukraine support.
insights.quote: stoke German angst about war and horizontal escalation, weaken centrist parties, and scare Berlin off military aid to Ukraine, knowing that if the German pillar cracks, European support could collapse with it
insights.locator: Yet the country’s deep-seated unease with power

insights.claim: Hans-Peter Schwarz's 1985 framing - that Germans moved from Machtbesessenheit (power obsession) to Machtvergessenheit (power oblivion) - remains the diagnostic for German strategic behaviour four decades on.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: A compact model for predicting German behaviour in crises: expect institutional and legalistic responses first, hard-power responses only under extreme forcing.
insights.quote: the political scientist Hans-Peter Schwarz already spoke of ‘the tamed Germans’, who, once driven by Machtbesessenheit (power obsession), had drifted into Machtvergessenheit (power oblivion)
insights.locator: By 1985, the political scientist Hans-Peter Schwarz

insights.claim: Germany's two founding maxims - 'Never Again Fascism' and 'Never Again Germany' - coexisted tolerably through the Cold War but have been placed in direct conflict by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, because anti-fascism now requires German power rather than German restraint.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: This is the actual fault line to watch inside German politics; how it resolves determines the ceiling on German defence spending and risk tolerance.
insights.quote: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has opened a faultline at the heart of German identity, revealing a clash between ‘Never Again Fascism’ and ‘Never Again Germany’.
insights.locator: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has opened a faultline

insights.claim: Germany treated Russia as a projection of its own biases rather than analysing it, missing that Russian strategic elites envisaged a Moscow-Berlin axis modelled on the 1922 Rapallo Treaty explicitly designed to pull Europe away from the United States.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Reconciliation framing masked a geopolitical programme; the same asymmetry of intent should be assumed in any future Russo-German energy or diplomatic rapprochement.
insights.quote: a Moscow-Berlin axis, inspired by the model of the 1922 Rapallo Treaty, as the core for a new European order, designed to pull Europe away from the United States
insights.locator: Sober analysis would have recognised

insights.claim: Germany's belief that Ostpolitik won the Cold War - rather than Soviet military overreach, a failing economy and the cost of propping up the socialist empire - supplied the intellectual cover for decades of hard-power abstention.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Historical narratives function as policy constraints; the contest over Cold War causation is a live driver of current German defence politics.
insights.quote: This overlooks less convenient explanations – that the Soviet Union collapsed under the collective weight of military overreach, a failing economy and the increasingly untenable costs of propping up its socialist empire.
insights.locator: Many credited Cold War victory to Brandt’s Ostpolitik

insights.claim: Germany for years assumed Moscow would neither launch a full-scale war nor weaponise energy, citing the reliability of Soviet deliveries during the Cold War - and both assumptions collapsed, making the costs of underestimating the Kremlin far exceed the risks of overestimating it.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: An explicit asymmetric-payoff argument for pricing Russia risk pessimistically - relevant to European energy security and any re-engagement thesis on Russian gas.
insights.quote: Yet the costs of underestimating the Kremlin’s maliciousness far exceed the risks of overestimation.
insights.locator: Berlin has repeatedly misread an adversary

insights.claim: Even after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, Germany remained in geopolitical self-denial, recognising the end of the 'end of history' only after the full-scale invasion and Moscow's failed gas blackmail - an eight-year lag between evidence and adjustment.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: German strategic adjustment lags evidence by years, so current policy likely still understates the next shock.
insights.locator: Yet so powerful and alluring was the vision

insights.claim: If Ukraine falls the Baltics could be next, and NATO's Article 5 - the foundation of German security for 71 years - would be tested as never before, forcing Germans to choose between sending troops and watching their core guarantee erode.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Frames Ukrainian battlefield outcomes as a direct input to the credibility of the entire European security guarantee, not a peripheral conflict.
insights.quote: If Ukraine falls, the Baltics could be next, and NATO’s Article 5 – the foundation of the Federal Republic’s security for 71 years – will be tested like never before.
insights.locator: The war already poses a serious

insights.claim: A resilient Ukraine is Germany's cheapest defence because any Russian attack on the Baltics would have to reckon with a vast front held by a battle-hardened army determined to liberate occupied territory.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Reframes aid to Ukraine as a capital-efficient substitute for German force structure - an argument that should survive fiscal tightening.
insights.quote: A resilient Ukraine is the best defence for both the Baltics and Germany.
insights.locator: They are mistaken

insights.claim: With France and Britain consumed by domestic political and financial crises, Germany is the only European power with both the fiscal capacity and the industrial strength to sustain Ukraine and contain Russia.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Concentration risk: European defence of Ukraine now depends on one country's budget politics, making German coalition arithmetic a tradeable macro variable.
insights.quote: While France and Britain appear to be consumed by domestic crises, political and financial, Germany has the fiscal capacity and industrial strength to rise to the challenge.
insights.locator: German power is crucial to sustaining Ukraine

insights.claim: Germany has for more than three years watched Russian shadow-fleet tankers transit the Baltic under cover of the law of the sea and answered drone incursions over Poland with sermons about international law - responses the Kremlin demonstrably discounts.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Legalistic responses have not deterred; expect either escalating Russian hybrid activity in the Baltic or a discontinuous German policy shift, with shipping and insurance implications either way.
insights.quote: met Russian drone incursions over Poland with tired sermons about the ‘lack of respect for international law’. The Kremlin could not care less about such pieties.
insights.locator: Friedrich Merz recognises this

insights.claim: After Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace in September 2025, Trump declared future intruders could be shot down and no further violations followed - a documented instance of explicit deterrence working against Moscow.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that credible, explicit threats change Russian behaviour cheaply - supports expecting more red-line declarations from European capitals.
insights.quote: after Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace in September 2025, Trump declared that future intruders could be shot down. None followed.
insights.locator: There is a telling precedent

insights.claim: Merz should privately signal to the Kremlin that any repeat of the Leipzig airport drone incident would trigger delivery of Taurus missiles to Ukraine, converting a weapons decision into a deterrence instrument.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable policy proposal - Taurus transfer is the single clearest observable signal that Germany has shifted to active deterrence.
insights.quote: Friedrich Merz should privately signal to the Kremlin that any incidents similar to what happened at the Leipzig airport would trigger the delivery of Taurus missiles to Ukraine
insights.locator: Attributing the Leipzig airport drone incident

insights.claim: France and Britain have sent personnel to Kyiv to help guide Storm Shadow and SCALP strikes while Germany refused Taurus on the grounds it would require German soldiers in Ukraine - and it is no coincidence that Europe's two nuclear powers accept greater risk.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Nuclear status directly sets conventional risk appetite; a useful predictor of which European states will escalate and which will hedge.
insights.quote: It is no coincidence that Europe’s two nuclear powers are willing to take greater risks.
insights.locator: In office, Merz abandoned his earlier push

insights.claim: Scholz's Zeitenwende in practice reverted to outsourcing strategic decisions to Washington, with a token Abrams pledge used to cover the Leopard tank decision so Germany could claim it acted 'always together and never alone' - a script the author says is now exhausted.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Germany can no longer hide decisions behind US cover as Washington disengages, forcing either autonomous German choices or visible paralysis.
insights.quote: Washington eased his resistance with a token pledge of Abrams tanks, allowing Scholz to claim Germany acted ‘always together and never alone’. That script is now exhausted.
insights.locator: Germany needs its own Ukraine strategy

insights.claim: The Baltic states have run a workable model since 1991 - probe, push back, draw lines, avoid escalation - while Russia has spent years 'boiling the German frog', widening its room for manoeuvre incrementally.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Incremental salami-slicing is the actual Russian method; monitor cumulative tolerance drift rather than discrete incidents.
insights.quote: Russia, meanwhile, has spent years boiling the German frog — turning up the heat and widening its room for manoeuvre.
insights.locator: This is the measured game

themes.theme: The German bomb - and how to buy one

insights.claim: Without a nuclear deterrent Germany is structurally vulnerable to blackmail, and the author argues nothing short of a German nuclear capability can supply credible mutually assured destruction against Moscow.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: The most against-consensus claim in mainstream European strategic writing; if it gains traction it reprices the entire European non-proliferation and defence complex.
insights.quote: It is difficult to see how anything short of a German nuclear capability could supply that credibility.
insights.locator: Long accustomed to wishing for the best possible outcome

insights.claim: A homegrown German bomb is dangerous because the gap between launching a programme and fielding weapons would be a phase of acute vulnerability inviting intensified Russian hybrid warfare, explicit threats, even strikes on the programme itself.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: The transition window, not the end state, is where the tail risk sits - the same logic applies to any state contemplating latent-to-overt nuclear breakout.
insights.quote: The gap between launching a programme and fielding weapons would be a phase of acute vulnerability, inviting intensified Russian hybrid warfare, explicit threats, even strikes against the programme itself.
insights.locator: Pursuing a homegrown bomb is dangerous, however

insights.claim: France could be won over by granting Germany operational control of warheads drawn from a French pool while Paris retains strict material oversight - structurally mirroring Britain's dependence on American-built Trident missiles.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Provides the specific legal-technical architecture a Franco-German nuclear arrangement would take, which is what to watch for in defence communiques.
insights.quote: warheads and delivery systems would be drawn from a French pool and sustained by French technical support — much as Britain depends on the United States for its American-built Trident missiles
insights.locator: Yet Germany has room to manoeuvre

insights.claim: France's domestic quagmire is pushing it towards a sovereign debt crisis while Germany retains the confidence of international capital markets, so a major German contribution to the French nuclear programme would let both governments trade security for fiscal space.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: The most directly tradeable idea in the piece: a German-funded French deterrent would be OAT-positive and is a concrete channel through which defence policy could relieve French fiscal stress.
insights.quote: France’s domestic quagmire pushes the country towards a sovereign debt crisis. Germany, by contrast, retains the confidence of international capital markets.
insights.locator: The offer could also be sweetened financially

insights.claim: The waning credibility of the US nuclear umbrella creates a commercial opening: a 'large, golden cheque' relieving America of a security burden could appeal to an administration loosely tied to traditional foreign policy principles, and Seoul officials already report Trump's inner circle appears open to allied nuclearisation if it reduces US commitments.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: If Washington monetises rather than defends non-proliferation, the number of nuclear-armed US allies could rise - a regime change for global security pricing, with South Korea as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: In Seoul, facing a similar predicament, officials note that Trump’s inner circle appears open to allied nuclearisation if it reduces US commitments.
insights.locator: Likewise, the waning credibility of the US nuclear umbrella

insights.claim: Germany should move first and demonstrate both the will and capacity to build a bomb, because confronted with a real German programme Paris and Washington might prefer to retain influence and profits rather than watch the world's third largest economy go it alone.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: A negotiating-leverage model: credible threat of indigenous development is the price-setting mechanism for acquiring an arsenal from allies.
insights.quote: Germany should move first and demonstrate to its allies both the will and the capacity to build a bomb.
insights.locator: Germany should move first

themes.theme: Domestic politics as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Embracing Machtpolitik is awkward precisely because the AfD leads in national polls, yet the author insists democratic Germany needs a 'double victory' at home and abroad, since defeat abroad would strengthen extremists claiming to hold the key to the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Foreign and domestic risk are coupled: a bad Ukraine outcome mechanically boosts the AfD, and AfD strength mechanically weakens Ukraine support - a reflexive loop to monitor.
insights.quote: for democratic Germany, there is no alternative to double victory, at home and abroad
insights.locator: It is an awkward moment to embrace Machtpolitik

insights.claim: Fascism and the spirit of revenge fester in humiliated societies such as Russia after 1991 and Germany after 1919 - meaning fascism is a product of humiliation rather than anything intrinsic to German national identity.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Relocates the fascism risk from Berlin to Moscow, which is the analytical move required to unlock German rearmament politically.
insights.quote: fascism and the spirit of revenge fester in humiliated societies such as Russia after 1991, just as it did in Germany after 1919
insights.locator: A return to Machtpolitik requires trust

insights.claim: Merz has spent political capital shielding Kyiv from Trump and rallying Europe behind the use of Russia's frozen assets, but on the author's reading he is not ahead of the curve and should also cast off the one-sided shackles of international law.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Use of Russian frozen assets is the near-term policy fight with the most direct financial consequences; Germany is the pivotal actor on it.
insights.quote: attempting to rally Europe behind the use of Russia’s frozen assets and reinforcing the material base of German power
insights.locator: Chancellor Merz has grasped the gravity of the moment

insights.claim: German foreign policy still clings to a legalistic worldview treating multilateralism as a universal reference point; the author argues Berlin should instead prioritise core interests in Eastern Europe and openly accept its limits elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: A prescription for German strategic narrowing - expect reduced German bandwidth for non-European theatres if adopted.
insights.quote: Instead, Germany should prioritise core interests in Eastern Europe and accept its limits elsewhere.
insights.locator: It begins with a reorientation

insights.claim: By the Cold War's end roughly 4,200 Soviet tanks occupied East Germany, a concrete reality that kept West German minds focused on accepting the costs of deterrence - a discipline lost once the threat disappeared.
insights.speaker: Peter Sies
insights.so_what: Deterrence spending is sustained by visible proximate threat; without it, defence budgets decay regardless of stated doctrine.
insights.quote: By the Cold War’s end, about 4,200 Soviet tanks occupied East Germany, a reality that kept minds focused on accepting the costs of deterrence.
insights.locator: During the Cold War, ‘Never Again Fascism’
